mainTopic: Whether an animal's mouth counts like the owner's courtyard, fencing against grazing animals, and how an ox becomes a מועד
overview: The גמרא learns from the case of a dog that ate bread that an animal's mouth counts like the injured party's courtyard. This matters because there was an open question: is a cow's mouth (פי פרה) like the injured party's courtyard or like the owner's? It attacks the 'owner's courtyard' side by asking when anyone would ever pay for שן. רב מרי answers with damage done for pleasure without the mouth. רבינא and רב אשי defend him against מר זוטרא's demand for total destruction. Proofs from a dog or snake set on a person are pushed off, because the argument 'what were you doing in my area?' does not apply where someone was killed. A ברייתא about an ox that kills a trespasser shows this. Then a story about goats that damaged רב יוסף's property teaches that a landowner is expected to fence his field. A public ruling adds that owners of damaging market goats are warned and then made to slaughter them. Finally a new משנה gives the מחלוקת between רבי יהודה and רבי מאיר on how an ox becomes a מועד. The גמרא brings the פסוק-based sources of אביי and רבא for רבי יהודה, and begins quoting רבי מאיר's source, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The dog's mouth counts like the injured party's courtyard
steps.stepSummary: From the ruling that the dog's owner pays for the bread, the גמרא learns that a dog's mouth is treated like the courtyard of the injured party.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like the courtyard of the injured party. Because if it were like the courtyard of the one who caused the damage, the owner could say to him: 'What is your bread doing in my dog's mouth?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an inference from the משנה: since the dog's owner must pay for the bread it ate, a dog's mouth must count like the injured party's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the dog's mouth counted as the owner's own space, the bread would be eaten 'in the owner's property.' Then the owner could escape paying by saying, 'Your bread had no business being in my dog's mouth.' Since the משנה makes him pay, the mouth cannot be treated as the owner's space.

keyTerms.meaning: The courtyard (property) of the person who was damaged
The courtyard (property) of the one responsible for the damage, here the animal's owner
It is considered like / it resembles

phrases.english: is like the courtyard of the injured party;
for if it were like the courtyard of the one who caused the damage,
let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The dog's owner would say this to the person whose bread was eaten.

phrases.english: What is your bread doing in my dog's mouth?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי כַּחֲצַר הַמַּזִּיק דָּמֵי, לֵימָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an inference drawn from the משנה of the dog that took bread.
steps.raayaObject: That an animal's mouth counts like the courtyard of the injured party
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's ruling that the dog's owner pays for the bread the dog ate

steps.title: The open question about a cow's mouth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the inference matters: there was an open question about whether a cow's mouth is like the injured party's courtyard or like the owner's.
steps.simpleTranslation: For they asked: is a cow's mouth like the courtyard of the injured party, or is it like the courtyard of the one who caused the damage?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows why the inference in step 1 is useful. It quotes a question that had been asked about a cow's mouth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether an animal's mouth is treated like the owner's private space or like the place where the food was taken from. The inference from the dog's case could help answer this open question.

keyTerms.meaning: It was asked of them; a question raised in the בית מדרש

phrases.english: For it was asked of them:
Is a cow's mouth like the courtyard of the injured party,
or is it like the courtyard of the one who caused the damage?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the background question that gives step 1's inference its importance.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an animal's mouth counts as the injured party's space or the owner's space

steps.title: If the mouth is the owner's space, when would שן ever apply?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the side that says the mouth is like the owner's courtyard: then no case of שן would ever make the owner pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say it is like the courtyard of the one who caused the damage, then how can you find a case of שן, for which the Torah makes the owner pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is challenging one side of the question from step 2.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner pays for שן only when the eating happens in the injured party's property. If the mouth always counts as the owner's space, every bite would happen 'at home,' and the Torah's rule about שן would have no case where the owner pays.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'tooth'; the category of damage an animal causes by eating or by acting for its own pleasure
How can you find it? Where would this case ever happen?

phrases.english: And if you say it is like the courtyard of the one who caused the damage,
then שן, for which the Torah makes the owner pay,
how can you ever find a case of it?
phrases.notes: Payment for שן applies only when the damage happens in the injured party's property, so every bite would be 'in the owner's space.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second side of the question in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that an animal's mouth is like the owner's courtyard
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If so, all eating happens in the owner's space, so the Torah's payment for שן would never apply.

steps.title: רב מרי: שן without the mouth
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא answers that the owner can still pay for שן when the animal damages for its own pleasure without using its mouth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי, son of רב כהנא, said: for example, when the cow rubbed against a wall for its pleasure, or dirtied produce for its pleasure.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי answers the challenge from step 3 by giving cases of שן that would still make the owner pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שן covers more than eating. It also covers any damage an animal does for its own pleasure. Rubbing against a wall or dirtying produce involves no mouth, so the damage clearly happens in the injured party's property, and the owner pays even if the mouth counts as the owner's space.
steps.whatToRemember: Even if an animal's mouth counts as the owner's space, שן still has real cases: damage the animal does for its own pleasure without its mouth, such as rubbing against a wall or dirtying produce.
steps.confusionAlert: שן does not only mean biting or eating. It covers any damage an animal does for its own enjoyment, even with no teeth involved.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Mari, son of Rav Kahana, said:
For example, when it rubbed against a wall for its pleasure,
or dirtied produce for its pleasure.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא: כְּגוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives other cases where the law applies
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed שן only means eating, so if the mouth is the owner's space, שן could never apply.
steps.terutzMaskana: שן includes damage done for the animal's pleasure without the mouth, and in those cases the owner pays.

steps.title: מר זוטרא: שן Must Destroy Completely
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא objects to רב מרי's examples. To count as שן, the damage must completely destroy the item, and in those examples it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא objected: But for שן I need 'as the tooth consumes until it is all gone,' meaning total destruction, and that is missing here!
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא attacks the answer from step 4. He says the examples of damage without the mouth do not fully destroy anything, so they cannot count as שן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 saved the 'owner's courtyard' view with cases where the animal damages for pleasure without using its mouth. מר זוטרא says the פסוק teaches that שן means the item is completely wiped out. A wall that was rubbed against or produce that was dirtied is still there, so these are not real שן cases.

keyTerms.meaning: He objected to it (a strong challenge)
Tooth: the damage category where an animal damages for its own pleasure

phrases.english: Mar Zutra objects to it:
phrases.notes: He is challenging רב מרי's answer from step 4 about damage done without the mouth.

phrases.english: But I require
"As the tooth consumes until it is all gone,"
phrases.notes: מלכים א 14:10. The גמרא reads this פסוק as saying שן must wipe the item out completely.

phrases.english: and that is not here!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מרי's examples of שן done without the mouth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שן requires total destruction (עד תמו). Rubbing a wall or dirtying produce leaves the item in existence, so these cases are not שן.

steps.title: רבינא and רב אשי Show Total Destruction
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the animal rubbed off pictures on the wall completely. רב אשי says it trampled the produce completely.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: It is where the animal rubbed out the pictures on the wall. רב אשי said: It is where the animal trampled the produce until it was crushed.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים defend רב מרי by showing that those non-mouth cases can involve full destruction after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא explains the wall case: the animal rubbed against a painted wall and erased the pictures completely. רב אשי explains the produce case: the animal stomped it until it was ruined. Both cases now meet the 'עד תמו' rule, so the question about the mouth stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Pictures or images (decorations on a wall)

steps.whyThisMatters: Because רב מרי's answer survives, the side that says the mouth is like the owner's courtyard is still possible, and the גמרא must look for another proof.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
where it rubbed off pictures,
Rav Ashi said:
where it trampled it thoroughly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers מר זוטרא's objection from step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case so it fits the requirement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The non-mouth cases leave the item intact, so they cannot be שן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The cases involve full destruction (erased pictures, crushed produce), so they are valid שן, and owners can still pay for שן even if the mouth is like their own courtyard.

steps.title: Proof from Inciting a Dog
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says someone who incites a dog is exempt, which seems to mean the dog's owner pays. If the mouth were like the owner's courtyard, the owner could say: 'What was your hand doing in my dog's mouth?'
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone set a dog or a snake on another person, he is exempt. Who is exempt? The one who incited is exempt, but the dog's owner must pay. If the mouth is like the owner's courtyard, the owner should be able to say: What was your hand doing in my dog's mouth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to settle the open question from step 2. It tries to prove the mouth is like the injured person's courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא reads 'exempt' as meaning only the inciter is free, while the dog's owner pays. If the dog's mouth counted as the owner's private space, the owner could argue that the victim put his hand into the owner's property. Since the owner still pays, the mouth must be like the victim's courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: He incited or urged on (an animal)
The courtyard of the one responsible for the damage

steps.confusionAlert: The proof depends on reading 'פטור' as referring only to the inciter. The next step questions exactly that reading.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If he incited the dog against him,
or incited the snake against him, he is exempt.
Who is exempt? The one who incited is exempt,
but the dog's owner is liable;
and if you say it is like the damager's courtyard,
let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The dog's owner says this to the injured person.

phrases.english: What is your hand doing in my dog's mouth?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: שִׁיסָּה בּוֹ אֶת הַכֶּלֶב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Once the attack on the 'owner's courtyard' view (step 3) is answered (steps 4-6), the גמרא brings a new source to settle the question.
steps.raayaObject: That an animal's mouth is like the injured person's courtyard
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about inciting a dog or snake (סנהדרין 66b), read as making the dog's owner liable

steps.title: Two Ways to Reject the Dog Proof
steps.stepSummary: First answer: 'exempt' includes the inciter too, so the owner may also be exempt. Second answer: the dog stuck out its teeth and scratched, so the hand was never inside its mouth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: even the one who incited is exempt. Or if you prefer, say: the dog pushed out its teeth and scratched him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from step 7 with two different answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First answer: read the ברייתא as 'even the inciter is exempt.' The owner is exempt too, which fits the view that the mouth is like the owner's courtyard. Second answer: even if the owner pays, the dog scratched with its outer teeth, so the victim's hand was never in the dog's mouth and the courtyard argument does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces a second answer

phrases.english: Say: even the one who incited is exempt.
And if you wish, say:
that it stuck out its fangs and scratched him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof completely, with two separate answers
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed that 'פטור' meant only the inciter and that the victim's hand was inside the dog's mouth. Both assumptions can be challenged.

steps.title: New Source: Making a Snake Bite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces another source: if someone makes a snake bite a person, רבי יהודה holds him liable and חכמים exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone made the snake bite a person, רבי יהודה holds him liable, and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to try again to settle the question. This is a setup line, and the reasoning comes in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case continues the same משנה about inciting animals. Here the person actually brought the snake's fangs to the victim. The גמרא will next explain how this מחלוקת relates to the status of the animal's mouth.

keyTerms.meaning: Caused to bite (brought the snake's fangs to the victim)

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: הִשִּׁיךְ בּוֹ אֶת הַנָּחָשׁ –
phrases.english: Come and hear: If he made the snake bite him,
Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable,
and the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הִשִּׁיךְ בּוֹ אֶת הַנָּחָשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the dog proof was rejected in step 8, the גמרא brings another source from the same משנה.
steps.raayaObject: The status of an animal's mouth (the proof is completed in step 11)
steps.raayaSupportSource: The מחלוקת between רבי יהודה and חכמים about one who makes a snake bite

steps.title: רב אחא בר יעקב explains the snake dispute
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב explains the snake dispute. For רבי יהודה the venom sits between the teeth, so the person who made it bite is killed by the sword and the snake is exempt. For חכמים the snake releases venom by itself, so the snake is stoned and the person is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר יעקב said: When you look into it, you find this. According to רבי יהודה, a snake's venom sits ready between its teeth. So the one who made it bite is killed by the sword, and the snake is exempt. According to חכמים, the snake spits out its venom on its own. So the snake is stoned, and the one who made it bite is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב אחא בר יעקב to explain the reasoning behind the snake dispute from the last step. This explanation sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole dispute depends on one question: who actually does the killing? If the venom is already sitting in the teeth, the person who pushed the snake is the real killer, like someone holding a sword. If the snake has to release the venom itself, the snake is the killer and gets stoned like any animal that kills a person.

keyTerms.meaning: The person who makes the snake bite someone
Sword, here meaning the death penalty by sword given to a murderer
Stoning, the death penalty given to an animal that kills a person
Spits it out by itself, so the snake releases the venom on its own

phrases.english: And Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
When you look into it, you will find:
According to Rabbi Yehuda,

phrases.aramaic: אֶרֶס נָחָשׁ – בֵּין שִׁינָּיו הוּא עוֹמֵד,
phrases.english: a snake's venom sits between its teeth,
therefore the one who made it bite is killed by the sword,
and the snake is exempt.
According to the Rabbis,
a snake spits out its venom on its own,
therefore the snake is stoned,
and the one who made it bite is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב: כְּשֶׁתִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the רבי יהודה / חכמים dispute brought in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever actually releases the venom is the killer: the person according to רבי יהודה, the snake according to חכמים.

steps.title: If the mouth were like the owner's courtyard, the owner could object
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws the proof. According to חכמים the snake is stoned. But if an animal's mouth counted like the owner's courtyard, the owner could say: 'What was your hand doing in my snake's mouth?' Since the snake is still stoned, the mouth seems not to count like his courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say an animal's mouth is like the damager's courtyard, let the owner say to him: What is your hand doing in my snake's mouth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the snake case to attack the idea that an animal's mouth counts like the owner's courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the mouth were like the owner's property, the victim would be the one who came into the owner's area, and the owner could push the blame onto him. Yet the snake is still stoned, so this argument seems not to work. That suggests the mouth is not like the owner's courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: The cow's mouth, standing for any animal's mouth
Like the courtyard of the one who caused the damage

phrases.english: And if you say
that the mouth of the cow is like the damager's courtyard,
let him say to him:
What is your hand doing in my snake's mouth?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ פִּי פָרָה כַּחֲצַר הַמַּזִּיק דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ruling of חכמים explained in step 10 as a proof against פי פרה כחצר המזיק.
steps.raayaObject: That an animal's mouth is not treated like the owner's courtyard.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling of חכמים that the snake is stoned, as explained by רב אחא בר יעקב.

steps.title: That argument is not used where someone was killed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof. The 'what were you doing in my area?' argument is never used in a case of killing, so the snake case says nothing about whether the mouth is like the courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Regarding killing, we do not say this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from the snake. The 'what were you doing in my area' argument simply does not apply when someone was killed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumed that if the mouth were like the courtyard, the snake would be saved. The גמרא answers that in a death case this argument does not work at all. So the snake is stoned either way, and the case proves nothing about the mouth.

keyTerms.meaning: In matters of killing or the death penalty

phrases.english: Regarding killing
we do not say this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof made in step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the snake case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the 'what were you doing in my area' argument could apply to a killing. It cannot.

steps.title: Source: an ox kills a trespasser
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source that the argument is not used in death cases. It brings a ברייתא: a person enters a courtyard without permission and the owner's ox gores him to death. The ox is stoned, but the owner is exempt from כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do you say this? As it was taught: If someone enters a homeowner's courtyard without permission, and the homeowner's ox gores him and he dies, the ox is stoned, and the owners are exempt from the ransom payment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how we know the rule from step 12, and brings a ברייתא to support it. This sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא gives a case where the victim really was on the owner's property without permission. It has two results: the ox is still put to death, but the owner does not pay כופר. The next steps explain why these two results differ.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do you say this? (asking for a source)
Ransom payment the owner of a dangerous ox pays when it kills a person

phrases.english: And from where do you say this?
As it was taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: הַנִּכְנָס לַחֲצַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת,
phrases.english: One who enters a homeowner's courtyard without permission,
and the homeowner's ox gored him,
and he died:
the ox is stoned,
and the owners are exempt from the ransom payment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies a source for the rule stated in step 12.
steps.raayaObject: That the 'what were you doing in my area' argument does not work in death cases.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about an ox that gores a trespasser to death.

steps.title: Why the owner pays no ransom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the owner is exempt from כופר: he can tell the victim, 'What were you doing on my property?'
steps.simpleTranslation: The owners are exempt from the ransom. What is the reason? Because he can say to him: What were you doing in my property?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the owner does not pay כופר and answers: the victim came in without permission. This sets up the challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner's exemption from כופר rests on the 'what were you doing in my area' argument. That shows this argument does work for the money payment.

keyTerms.meaning: In my property or my domain
What were you doing? What did you want? (here: you had no business being there)

phrases.english: The owners are exempt from the ransom payment;
what is the reason?
Because he says to him:
What were you doing in my property?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָלִים פְּטוּרִין מִן הַכּוֹפֶר מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second half of the ברייתא from step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the owner is exempt from כופר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because the victim was on the owner's property without permission.

steps.title: Then the ox should be spared too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא presses: if that argument frees the owner from כופר, it should also save the ox. Yet the ברייתא says the ox is stoned.
steps.simpleTranslation: His ox too: let him say to him, What were you doing in my property!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a problem. The same argument that frees the owner should also save the ox, but the ox is still stoned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both results come from the same case of trespassing. If 'what were you doing here' works for the money, why doesn't it work for the ox's death? The question shows there must be a difference between money and death.

phrases.english: His ox too:
let him say to him:
What were you doing in my property!

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוֹרוֹ נָמֵי, לֵימָא לֵיהּ: מַאי בָּעֵית בִּרְשׁוּתִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the reason from step 14 to raise a difficulty about the ox being stoned in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the ox is stoned.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The argument that frees the owner from כופר should also save the ox.

steps.title: Conclusion: the argument does not apply to killing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that 'what were you doing in my area' is not used in death cases. That is why the ox is stoned, and why the snake case proves nothing about פי פרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, regarding killing, we do not say this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question and closes the proof. The 'my property' argument does not apply to death, so the ox is still stoned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument works for money (the owner pays no כופר) but not for putting the animal to death. This proves the rule from step 12. So the snake case cannot show whether an animal's mouth is like the owner's courtyard.
steps.whatToRemember: The 'what were you doing on my property?' argument can free an owner from paying, like the כופר, but it never stops a killer animal from being put to death. So death cases cannot prove whether פי פרה כחצר המזיק.

phrases.english: Rather, regarding killing
we do not say this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the difficulty in step 15 and confirms the rejection in step 12.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The 'my property' argument does not apply to death penalties. So neither the ox case nor the snake case proves anything about פי פרה כחצר המזיק.

steps.title: Goats damage רב יוסף's property
steps.stepSummary: Goats belonging to the house of תרבו kept damaging רב יוסף's property. He asked אביי to tell the owners to keep them locked up.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were goats from the בית תרבו family that kept causing damage to רב יוסף. He told אביי: go tell their owners to keep them shut in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about goats that damage someone's property. It is setting up the question of who must prevent the damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף assumes the goat owners are responsible. They should keep their goats away from other people's land. The next step will challenge that assumption.

keyTerms.meaning: They should put them away (keep them locked up)

phrases.english: There were these goats of the Tarbu family
that kept causing damage to Rav Yosef.
He said to Abaye:
Go and tell their owners
that they should keep them shut away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of 'what were you doing in my area' ended in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף assumes the goat owners must keep their goats from damaging others.

steps.title: אביי says the owners will tell him to build a fence
steps.stepSummary: אביי refuses to go. He says the owners will answer that רב יוסף should fence in his own land.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Why should I go? If I go, they will tell me, 'Let the Master build a fence on his own land.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers רב יוסף. He explains that the owners have a good reply: the victim should protect his own field with a fence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's point is that for eating damage (שן), the burden falls on the landowner to fence his field. If he did not fence it, he cannot easily complain to the animal's owner. This shifts the responsibility from the damager to the victim.

phrases.english: He said to him: Why should I go?
For if I go, they will say to me:
Let the Master put up a fence on his land.
phrases.notes: 'The Master' means רב יוסף himself; this is a polite way of speaking about him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רב יוסף's request and pushes back on it.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The landowner is expected to fence his field against animals that eat.

steps.title: Then when is the owner ever liable for eating damage?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי's idea. If the victim always has to fence, when would the Torah's liability for שן ever apply?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he did build a fence, how could you ever find a case of שן where the Torah makes the owner pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea that the victim must fence his land. If he fences, animals cannot get in. So when would the Torah's law of paying for שן ever apply?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah clearly makes an owner pay when his animal eats in someone else's field. If the victim had to fence and the animals still could not get in, that law would never come up. So אביי's claim seems to wipe out a Torah law.

keyTerms.meaning: Tooth: damage an animal does by eating for its own benefit
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
How can you find it? (When could this case ever happen?)

phrases.english: And if he did put up a fence,
the damage of Eating, which the Torah makes the owner pay for,
how can you ever find a case of it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי גָּדַר, שֵׁן דְּחַיֵּיב רַחֲמָנָא הֵיכִי מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's claim that the landowner must fence his field.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that the victim is expected to fence his land.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a fence is required and it keeps animals out, the Torah's liability for שן would never apply.

steps.title: Cases where a fenced field is still damaged
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with two cases. The animal dug under the fence, or the fence fell down at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: It can happen when the animal dug under the fence. Or when the fence fell down at night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. It shows that even when the victim did his part by fencing, an animal can still get in and eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's law of שן still applies in cases where the victim did fence his field, but the fence failed. One case is an animal digging under it. Another is the fence falling at night, before the owner could fix it. So אביי's position stands, and the Torah law still has cases where it applies.

keyTerms.meaning: It (the animal) dug or burrowed under

phrases.english: When it dug under the fence.
Or else, when the fence fell down at night.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּשֶׁחָתְרָה. אִי נָמֵי, דְּנָפֵיל גּוּדָּא בְּלֵילְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the Torah's law to cases where the fence failed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the victim must fence, the law of שן would have no cases at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: The law of שן applies when the fence was dug under or fell at night, so the victim's duty to fence does not cancel it.
steps.whatToRemember: The victim is expected to fence his field against animals that eat. The animal owner pays for שן when the fence was dug under or fell at night.

steps.title: Public announcement about damaging market goats
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף (or רבה) announced a rule for goats in the market that cause damage. Warn the owner two or three times. If he does not listen, make him slaughter them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף, and some say רבה, announced: to all who go up and all who go down, about these market goats that cause damage, we warn their owner two or three times. If he listens, good. If not, we tell him: 'Go sit by the butcher's block and take your money.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a public ruling about goats in the market that keep damaging things. It describes the steps a court takes against their owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First the owner gets warned several times. If he keeps ignoring the warnings, he is told to slaughter the goats and sell the meat now. This works because the goats were going to be slaughtered anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: The butcher's block or slaughter place

phrases.english: Rav Yosef, and some say Rabba, would announce:
To those going up and those going down:
phrases.notes: He means scholars traveling between בבל and ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: These market goats that cause damage,
we warn their owner two or three times.
If he listens, he listens.
And if not, we say to him:
Sit by the butcher's block and take your money.
phrases.notes: In other words: slaughter your goats now and sell the meat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a practical ruling about damaging goats, on the same theme as the story of the תרבו goats.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Warn the owner of damaging market goats two or three times. If he ignores the warnings, force him to slaughter them.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the court can step in to stop ongoing damage, not just collect payment after it happens.
steps.whatToRemember: For goats that damage in the market, the court warns the owner a few times. If he ignores the warnings, it makes him slaughter them.

steps.title: New משנה: רבי יהודה on how an ox becomes known to gore
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks what a תם is and what a מועד is. רבי יהודה says an ox becomes a מועד after witnesses testify it gored on three days. It goes back to תם after three days of not goring.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which ox is a תם and which is a מועד? A מועד is any ox that witnesses testified about for three days. It goes back to being a תם once it stops for three days. These are the words of רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It asks how an ox gets the status of מועד, and how it loses that status. It starts with רבי יהודה's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, the count depends on days. The ox becomes a מועד after goring on three separate days. It becomes a תם again after three days in a row without goring.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox not yet known to gore; its owner pays only half the damage
An ox known to gore; its owner pays full damage

phrases.english: MISHNA: Which ox is innocuous and which is forewarned?

phrases.aramaic: מוּעָד – כֹּל שֶׁהֵעִידוּ בּוֹ שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים,
phrases.english: Forewarned: any ox that witnesses testified about on three days,
and it is innocuous again once it stops for three days;
this is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: an ox becomes a מועד after goring on three days, and goes back to תם after three days without goring.
steps.confusionAlert: תם and מועד are both kinds of damaging ox (קרן). The difference is only how much the owner pays: half damage for a תם, full damage for a מועד.

steps.title: רבי מאיר's view of forewarned and innocuous
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says an ox becomes a מועד after goring three times, even on one day. It goes back to תם only when children can play with it and it does not gore.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: A מועד is one that witnesses testified gored three times. A תם is one that children can touch and play with, and it does not gore.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives רבי מאיר's opinion, which disagrees with רבי יהודה on both points.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי מאיר, what counts is the number of gorings, not the number of days. Getting back to תם is also stricter for him. Simply going three days without goring is not enough. The ox must be so calm that children can play with it safely.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
Forewarned: an ox that witnesses testified gored three times,

phrases.aramaic: וְתָם – כֹּל שֶׁיְּהוּ הַתִּינוֹקוֹת מְמַשְׁמְשִׁין בּוֹ
phrases.english: and innocuous: any ox that children can pet and play with
and it does not gore.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion to רבי יהודה in the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: three gorings make an ox a מועד, even on one day. It goes back to תם only if children can play with it and it does not gore.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה counts days: three days of goring make a מועד, and three quiet days make it a תם again. רבי מאיר counts times: three gorings make a מועד, and it is a תם again only when children can play with it safely.

steps.title: What is the source for רבי יהודה's three days?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה says an ox becomes a מועד only after goring on three separate days.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the reason of רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה by asking where רבי יהודה gets his rule of three separate days. It is setting up the answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's rule depends on days, not just the number of gorings. The גמרא wants to know which פסוק teaches that days are what count.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason? (What is the source?)
An ox that is not known to gore. The owner pays half damages.
An ox that has been warned about. The owner pays full damages.

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא on the משנה quoted in steps 22-23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for counting goring by separate days.

steps.title: אביי counts each word of the verse
steps.stepSummary: אביי reads ״תְּמֹל״, ״מִתְּמֹל״ and ״שִׁלְשֹׁם״ as three separate days of goring. ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ בְּעָלָיו״ is then the fourth goring, where full payment applies.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: "Yesterday" is one. "From yesterday" is two. "The day before yesterday" is three. "And its owner did not guard it" brings us to the fourth goring.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers by counting the words of the פסוק. Each time word stands for one day of goring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks in terms of days: yesterday, before yesterday. So רבי יהודה counts days, not just gorings. For אביי, three day-words mean three days of goring, and the owner pays full damages on the fourth goring.

keyTerms.meaning: And its owner did not guard it

steps.confusionAlert: The three day-words describe the gorings that already happened. The full-payment goring comes after them, so for אביי it is the fourth goring.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
"Yesterday" is one;
"From yesterday" is two;
"The day before yesterday" is three;
"And its owner did not guard it":
we have come to the fourth goring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק's three day-words mean three days of goring. Full liability comes on the fourth goring.

steps.title: רבא reads the verse with fewer counts
steps.stepSummary: רבא reads ״תְּמֹל–מִתְּמֹל״ together as one day and ״שִׁלְשֹׁם״ as two. ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ means the goring now, the third, and the owner is already liable for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: "Yesterday, from yesterday" is one. "The day before yesterday" is two. "And he did not guard it" means now, and he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different way to count the same פסוק. He makes the full-liability goring the third one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא does not split ״תְּמֹל״ and ״מִתְּמֹל״ into two days, because together they are one phrase. That gives only two past days of goring, and the present goring is the third. So for רבא, full payment starts on the third goring, not the fourth.
steps.whyThisMatters: אביי and רבא agree that רבי יהודה learns from the same פסוק. They disagree about which goring first gets full payment: the fourth (אביי) or the third (רבא).

phrases.english: Rava said:
"Yesterday, from yesterday" is one;
"The day before yesterday" is two;
"And he did not guard it" means now, and he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another reading of the same פסוק, different from אביי's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Two past days of goring, and the owner is already fully liable for the third goring.

steps.title: What is the source for רבי מאיר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי מאיר counts gorings and not days. It starts to quote a ברייתא with his words.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the reason of רבי מאיר? As it was taught: רבי מאיר said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks for רבי מאיר's source. It begins to quote a ברייתא, so this line is setting up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר says three gorings, even on one day, make an ox a מועד. That seems to go against a פסוק that speaks about days, so the גמרא needs his source. The answer continues in the ברייתא that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir, what is his reason?
As it was taught: Rabbi Meir said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רבי יהודה's source to רבי מאיר's source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for רבי מאיר's rule that counts gorings, not days.
